         CARPENTER LAND AND CATTLE CO.’S REPLIES TO EXCEPTIONS TO
                         PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

          Carpenter Land and Cattle Co. (Carpenter) files the Replies to Exceptions to the Proposal

  for Decision (PFD). Pursuant to the Exceptions and Replies Memorandum, filed on August 20,

  2026, these Replies are timely filed on or before September 9, 2026.

                                I.    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF REPLIES

          Carpenter primarily responds to the exceptions filed in support of the alternative

  recommendation of Route 894, which argue that the Commission should select Route 894 if it

  approves the Application. In addition, these replies to exceptions refute the assertion filed on

  behalf of Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed (Sneed) that support selection of Route 891. 1                        Multiple

  parties filed exceptions supporting Route 296,2 which Carpenter also supports. While there are



          1
              See Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed’s (“Sneed”) Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 3-4.
          2
            See e.g., G-9 and G-13 Landowners’ Exceptions to Proposal for Decision; John M Burrow’s Exception to
  PFD; Staten Creek Ranch Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision.
                                                                                           Page 3 of 14


multiple factors supporting selection of Route 296, these replies provide particular focus on the

Colorado River crossing issue of the various routes put forth by the parties in exceptions. Carpenter

supports the selection of Route 296 because it:

      avoids unnecessary and new habitat fragmentation by co-locating infrastructure at a
       preexisting, disturbed corridor with existing infrastructure that crosses the Colorado River;
      eliminates the visual impacts to Colorado Bend State Park and the recently acquired Post
       Oak Ridge State Park by being situated outside the viewscape for the benefit of Texans for
       generations;
      minimizes the engineering constraints, environmental and regulatory threats associated
       with installing a turning structure in immediate proximity of the Colorado River’s bank
       and disturbance of Greenwood Creek and area springs; and
      reduces the negative impacts to historic and generational properties throughout the Texas
       Hill County, specifically the Carpenter’s beloved Greenwood Creek Ranch.

       Although these replies focus on questions of routing, Carpenter supports the

recommendation in the PFD that recommends that the Commission deny the Application at this

time and require further analysis to determine if this proposed project would actual be necessary

to the meet the system needs based on current circumstances. To reduce redundancy, Carpenter

asks the Commission to refer back to its arguments on Cost, Prudent Avoidance, and Paralleling

in support of selection of Route 296 (or 296 Option A) in its exceptions and prior briefing. These

replies will focus primarily on the Colorado River crossing issue as it relates to Community Values,

Parks and Recreation, Environmental Integrity, Historical Values, and Engineering Constraints.

Additionally, Carpenter supports the need-based arguments presented in the Save the Lampasas’

replies to exceptions.
                                                                                                       Page 4 of 14


                                     II.     REPLIES TO EXCEPTIONS

A.       Community Values. Like Route 894, Route 891 is contrary to community values of
         historic, generational Ranches situated along the bank of the Colorado River near
         both Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park.

         Sneed argues that Route 891 is the superior option when considering the Commission’s

routing criteria.3 Proponents of Route 891 fail to properly consider the community value impacts

of selecting a route that would cross the Colorado River on Carpenter’s Greenwood Creek Ranch

and the adjacent Robby Vann’s Jigger Ranch—both of which have preserved the natural habitat

of the Colorado River for generations. However, this is only a plausible argument if they choose

to ignore the evidence that Route 894 crosses many generational ranches 4 and over the Colorado

River by cutting a new, previously undisturbed corridor is contrary to each of the applicable

statutory routing criteria.5 The record establishes that the Colorado River is a treasured community

resource, particularly the navigable portion of the river that would be crossed by proposed link J22

(which is part of Route 891 and 894).

         In fact, the first Order approving a 765 kV transmission line in Texas supports

consideration of the protection of the affected state parks and ensuring the continuity of

generational family ranches as community values. 6 The Order in PUC Docket No. 59315 contains

the following findings, which should be restated here:

     -   Among other things, community values in the study area include preserving rural living
         and unspoiled landscapes; ensuring the continuity of generational family ranches and other
         3
             Sneed’s Exceptions to the PFD at 3 (Sept. 2, 2026).
         4
             G-9 and G-13 Landowners Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 7-9.
         5
          See Yates Exceptions to the Proposal at 13 (indicating that Route 296 is farther from Colorado Bend State
Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park and Link J31 of Route 296 is the least worst option for crossing the Colorado
River.)
         6
           Application Of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC To Amend Its Certificate Of Convenience And
Necessity For The Dinosaur Switch-Longshore Switch 765-KV Transmission Line Project In Borden, Bosque, Brown,
Callahan, Coke, Coleman, Comanche, Eastland, Erath, Glasscock, Hamilton, Hood, Howard, Jones, Mitchell, Nolan,
Runnels, Shackelford, Somervell, Stephens, Sterling, And Taylor Counties, Docket 59315, Finding of Fact Nos. 93-95
(Aug. 28, 2026)
                                                                                                        Page 5 of 14


        farming and agricultural endeavors; maintaining access to recreational activities such as
        camping, fishing, swimming, and hunting; and avoiding conflicts with wildlife
        management areas. These values are pervasive throughout the study area and all routes for
        the proposed transmission facilities have positive and negative impacts;7

    -   The evidence establishes a widespread appreciation for [Colorado Bend and Post Oak
        Ridge] State Park by intervenors and the public at large; and

    -   Route [296] does not affect [Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge] State Park and adequately
        addresses the expressed community values, including recognition of the park as a shared
        resource. 8

        As noted in Carpenter’s prior briefing, protecting the native environment, the contributing

creeks to the Colorado River, and Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park are

significant community values. This is also displayed in the Direct Testimony of Robby Vann,

where he indicated that “… TPWD purchasing the north portion of the [Vann] ranch to become

Post Oak Ridge State Park fulfilled a desire to preserve our ranch’s scenic beauty and the

ranching legacy while sharing this beauty and natural wonder with all of Texas.”9 This was

confirmed by Governor Abbott when he attended the opening of Post Oak Ridge State Park, where

he stated it was “a great day for the future of Texas.” 10

more existing transmission lines and public roads, crosses less land of high historical-site potential, has a higher

approximately $4 million more expensive than Route 894 on a project approaching $1.7 billion - roughly one quarter
of one percent.”); Aaron Edward Howton - Exceptions to PFD at 3 (indicating other community values impacted by
Route 894).

Callahan, Coke, Coleman, Comanche, Eastland, Erath, Glasscock, Hamilton, Hood, Howard, Jones, Mitchell, Nolan,
Runnels, Shackelford, Somervell, Stephens, Sterling, And Taylor Counties, Docket 59315, Finding of Fact Nos. 93-95
(Aug. 28, 2026).

        10

with photo of Governor Abbott visiting Post Oak Ridge State Park).
                                                                                               Page 6 of 14




                                                                                         11



       Post Oak Ridge State Park would not exist as it does today without Vanns generational

protection of the environment coupled with their desire to share that value with all of Texas.12 The

Carpenters have also preserved and protected the surrounding area that extends to the viewshed of

Post Oak Ridge State Park for almost 100 years to the benefit of the community. 13 Without the

contributions of these two families, generations of Texans would not be able to enjoy this well-

preserved area of the hill country. Accordingly, any party that supports the selection of a route that

crosses the Colorado River on proposed Link J22 (i.e., Route 891 or 894) overlooks the value of

these ranches, the communities they support, and the impacts that will be faced by the Texans who

will explore these State Parks for the years to come.

       12

B.     Parks and Recreation. Crossing the Colorado River in the viewshed of Colorado Bend
       State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park introduces irreparable harm to recreation
       that can be avoided by Route 296.

       Like Route 894, the record shows that if Route 891 were selected, the line would be seen

from both Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park, leveraging the highest point

on the historic and preserved Carpenter property. 14 Despite this, none of the Exceptions attempt

to reconcile the PFD’s silence on the TPWD’s description of park impacts in setting the selected

route farther from the boundary of Post Oak Ridge State Park to protect the viewshed of the

headquarters, trailhead, and Post Oak Falls overlook, and Colorado Bend State Park. 15 In fact, other

supporters of Route 296 consider the PFD’s analysis on the river crossing defective as well. 16




                                                                                          17



       Nor do the proponents of Route 891 or 894 reconcile the evidence that crossing the

Colorado River on Link J22 is contrary to Commission precedent that is specific to this portion of

the Colorado River.


       14
            Carpenter Dir. at 15.
       15
            See Id. at Exhibit F.
       16

       17
            R. Vann Dir. at 36.

        In Docket No. 37448 (the Gillespie-to-Newton 345-kV CREZ transmission line

proceeding), the Commission evaluated routing options in the same study area as the current

project.18 In that proceeding, the Commission rejected proposed routes that came within one mile

of Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Falls.19 The Commission determined that such

proximity would compromise public use of the park and adversely affect local resources. 20 The

record shows that the crossings at issue here on Link J22 (Route 894 or 891) or J31 (Route 296)

are the same crossings that were considered and ultimately rejected by the Commission as failing

to comply with the applicable routing standards. 21




         18
            Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to Amend its Certificate of Convenience and
Necessity for the Gillespie to Newton 345-kV CREZ Transmission Line in Gillespie, Llano, San Saba, Burnet, and
Lampasas Counties, Texas, Docket No. 37448, Chairman Smitherman Memo (Apr. 22, 2010); Order (Apr. 28, 2010).

       Like Route 894, Link 891 relies on Link J22, which sits within a half-mile of Colorado

Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park. This layout places the transmission line closer to

park lands than the route segment the Commission rejected in Docket No. 37448. 22 Chairman

Smitherman testified that, during his tenure as PUC Chairman, he advised the Commission that he

rejected segment C20 in Docket No. 37448 because its proximity to Colorado Bend State Park and

Post Oak Falls would compromise park use.23 Smitherman’s direct testimony states that proposed

Links J22 and J26 cross the Colorado River in the same vicinity as the segments rejected in Docket




       22
            Docket No. 37448, Chairman Smitherman Memo.
       23
            Carpenter Ex. 5, Direct Testimony of Barry T. Smitherman (Smitherman Dir.) at 16.
                                                                                         Page 10 of 14


No. 37448.24 His testimony states that these crossings merit rejection, given the public investment

in the new Post Oak Ridge State Park.25 Route 296 avoids these conflict areas by crossing the river

at Link J31, which is several miles from the park boundaries. Therefore, Commission precedent

supports the rejection of Routes 891 and 894 and the selection of Route 296 because Route 296

maintains the necessary distance from state park properties to protect park use and scenic

resources.

C.       Aesthetic and Historic Values. Ranches along the Colorado River are the historic and
         aesthetic foundation for Post Oak Ridge State Park.

         For generations, the Carpenter Family, through Greenwood Creek Ranch, and the Vann

Family through Jigger Ranch, have preserved and protected the natural beauty of the Colorado

River.

Vann’s testimony states:

         “We were pleased to see that the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department recognized
         the pristine nature and scenic views of this rugged terrain that the Vann family has
         been fortunate to preserve for over 137 years. The TPWD purchasing the north
         portion of the ranch to become Post Oak Ridge State Park fulfilled a desire to
         preserve our ranch’s scenic beauty and the ranching legacy while sharing this
         beauty and natural wonder with all of Texas.” 26

         Jigger Ranch protects a significant portion of the east bank of the Colorado River

immediately south Post Oak Ridge State Park,27 and then Greenwood Creek Ranch picks ups

shortly thereafter. These two ranches have preserved the natural beauty of the Colorado River for

over 100 years for the benefit of its community and neighbors, all of which make up their historic

family legacy.

              Id.
         25
              Id.
         26
              R. Vann Dir. at 10.
         27

D.      Environmental Integrity. Route 296 excels in environmental metrics, and Routes 891
        and 894 fall short.

        Commission Staff and other intervenors acknowledge that Route 296 performs very well

when considering the environmental factors emphasized in the PFD. 28

        Moseley Group and the V8 Landowners argue that “Route 894’s crossing of the Colorado

River using Link J22 is superior to the Link U3” because J22 crosses in a “perpendicular

manner.”29 This is a red herring. They do not point to anything in the record indicating that any

crossing is set at a perfect 90-degree angle, that this exact angle is the preferred engineering method

for crossing major rivers, or that it is environmentally favorable. 30 Also, while U3 crosses an ESSS,

the record reflects that Route 894 also crosses an ESSS, just not at J22—but on G51/52.31

Additionally, characterizing J22 as an area without riverbeds is completely false. Assuming even

distribution, J22 has more than one stream crossing per mile, and U3 has less than one per mile . 32

The Carpenters sponsored the testimony of an expert witness who thoroughly documented the

surface and subsurface springs that would be severely detrimentally impacted by routes using Link

J22.33 Furthermore, while the EA table indicates that J22 does not cross designated USFWS

critical habitat, the record makes clear that the Greenwood Creek Ranch is home to endangered

             PUC Legal Division Exceptions at 15. Despite this acknowledgment, the PUC Staff argued that other
factors offset Route 296's superior performance on the statutory environmental-impact criteria. The other factors
referenced relate specifically to proximity to the Florence ISD school; G-9 and G-13 Landowners' Exceptions to the
Proposal for Decision at 10; see also Aaron Edward Howton - Exceptions to PFD at 4-5.
        29
             Moseley Group and the V8 Landowners’ Exceptions to the PFD at 2
        30

        31
           Reply Brief of Save the Lampasas at 8 (“…G51 and G52 would have severe impacts on the entire
Lampasas River Watershed area, especially Rocky Creek (which has been designated as an Ecologically Sensitive
Stream)”).
        32
            Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 23 (Combined Data Table) (U3 is 22.42 miles with 19 stream crossings and J22
is 7.95 miles with 9 river crossings) .
        33
             Carpenter Ex. 2, Hall Dir. at 5.
                                                                                                          Page 12 of 14


and protected species such as golden-cheeked warblers, bald eagles, 34 and black-capped vireos.35

Other supporters of Route 296 cite golden-cheeked warbler habitat and observations along Route

894.36 The Carpenters take great pride in their wildlife management program established to protect

these sensitive species from threats to their documented habitat range, as do many other ranches

situated on Route 894.37 The lack of USFWS critical habitat documentation in this proceeding was

discussed by expert Aaron Brewer, who clarified that “the golden-cheeked warblers have been

listed as endangered since 1990, but critical habitat has never been formally designated for it.” 38

E.      Engineering Constraints. The turning structure near the J22 Colorado River crossing
        poses a unique challenge to Route 894 that the Applicants, the ALJs, and other
        intervenors have overlooked.

        Not one of the Exceptions filed in favor of selecting Route 894 mentions that the J22 river

crossing requires a turning structure in close proximity to the Colorado River bank. Specifically,

Routes 894 and 891 require a turning structure on Greenwood Creek Ranch within close proximity

to the Colorado River.39

        As indicated in prior briefing, turning structures will require deeper excavation and

concrete footings than a new 765kV standard structure, which pose great concerns from a

groundwater intrusion perspective as well as an engineering perspective given the short distance

between it and the Colorado River.

             See also R. Vann Dir. at 13 (indicating bald eagle sittings along the Colorado River neat J22.).
        35
             Carpenter Dir. at 11-12.
        36
             Aaron Edward Howton - Exceptions to PFD at 4.

18, and 41-42.
        38
             Carpenter Ex. 4, Direct Testimony of Aaron Brewer (Brewer Dir.) at 23.
        39
             Carpenter Dir. at 18.
                                                                                       Page 13 of 14


F.     Prudent Avoidance. Commission precedent supports the selection of a route that
       better protects state parks even if it increases the number of habitable structures
       impacted by the route.

       It is important to note that Commission precedent clarifies that protection of the Colorado

River from being crossed at the sensitive location in proximity to the TPWD State Parks, despite

the fact that there is a somewhat higher habitable structure count than on Route 894. For example,

in Docket No. 38290, Application of Sharyland Utilities, LP to Amend its CCN for the 19 Proposed

Hereford to White Deer 345 - kV CREZ Transmission Line, where the Commission selected a route

with higher habitable structure numbers based on consideration of the avoidance of building in

proximity to Palo Duro Canyon.

                                    III.    CONCLUSION

       For these reasons, Carpenter respectfully requests that the Commission affirm the Proposal

for Decision determining that the Applicants have failed to meet the burden of proof that the line

is needed under PURA § 37.056. In the alternative, if the Commission rejects the primary

recommendation of the PFD, Carpenters request that the Commission reject Route 894 and select

Route 296 in favor of any other proposed route.
